prompt: Two copies of a database lose the link between them. A customer writes to one copy. What can that copy do, according to the CAP theorem?

choices.text: Accept the write and wait for the link to replicate it before answering
choices.why: Waiting for a link that is down is refusing, only slower.

choices.text: Refuse the write, or accept it without the other copy knowing
choices.why: Right: those are the only two moves.

choices.text: Accept it and guarantee both copies agree once the link returns
choices.why: Agreeing later is convergence; reads in the meantime can still disagree.

choices.text: Forward it to the other copy through the client
choices.why: Nothing in the theorem routes around a partition.

prompt: Which cost does PACELC add to what CAP already describes?

choices.text: The memory each copy needs
choices.why: PACELC is about copies agreeing, not about resources.

choices.text: The latency of waiting for other copies when the network is fine
choices.why: Right: the Else half.

choices.text: The time an election takes after a primary has failed
choices.why: Elections happen on failures; PACELC's second half is about ordinary days.

choices.text: The disk space used by replication logs
choices.why: Disk is not one of the two choices it names.

prompt: Two copies sit 6,000 km apart, joined by fibre where light covers about 200,000 km a second. A write waits for the far copy's acknowledgement. What is the least it can take, in milliseconds?
Lesson 1 asks, per operation, what a disagreement between copies would cost and what a refusal would cost. Which of the shop's operations come out on the side of consistency? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Taking the last monitor out of stock
choices.why: Right: a disagreement sells one unit twice.

choices.text: Charging the card for an order
choices.why: Right: a disagreement can charge the customer twice, and a refusal only makes the order wait.

choices.text: Adding an item to a basket
choices.why: A basket one item short for a second harms nobody; a refused basket stops the customer shopping.

choices.text: Counting a page view
choices.why: A count a few views behind is harmless, and this one wants latency as well.

choices.text: Showing "customers also bought"
choices.why: Slightly old suggestions beat an empty box.

prompt: A container that the kernel killed for lack of memory shows exit code ___ in `docker ps -a`.
Order 1001 is stored in Redis as a JSON string under `order:1001`. What happens with `HGET order:1001 total`?

choices.text: It returns the total, because Redis parses JSON
choices.why: To Redis the string is bytes.

choices.text: It returns nil, because the field is missing
choices.why: It is not missing; the key is the wrong type for the command.

choices.text: It is refused with WRONGTYPE
choices.why: Right: a field belongs to a hash, and this key holds a string.

choices.text: It converts the key into a hash and returns an empty value
choices.why: Redis never converts a key's type for you.

prompt: In Cassandra, `SELECT … WHERE unit_price > 500` on a table keyed by customer is refused. What does the refusal ask for?

choices.text: A secondary index on `unit_price`, created before the query is run again
choices.why: The message names another option.

choices.text: `ALLOW FILTERING`, accepting a read of every partition
choices.why: Right, and the message warns about unpredictable performance.

choices.text: A consistency level of `ALL`
choices.why: Consistency has nothing to do with filtering.

choices.text: Quoting the number as text
choices.why: The type is right; the shape of the question is the problem.

prompt: Match each family to what it keeps together.

pairs.right: the whole order with its lines inside
a value filed under one name
one customer's rows, sorted, in a partition
things and the links between them

right_distractors: each fact once, in its own table

prompt: A shop needs "every order over 500 reais" from a key-value design. Which approach is the key-value way?

choices.text: A sorted set scored by total, written beside each order
choices.why: Right: a second structure keeps the answer ready, at the cost of a second write.

choices.text: Run a query with a condition on the value
choices.why: There is no such command; the key is the only way in.

choices.text: Store the orders as hashes so Redis can compare the field
choices.why: A hash lets you read one field by key, not search by its value.

choices.text: Raise the memory limit so a full scan fits
choices.why: Memory does not create a command that searches values.

prompt: Why does the course store money in MongoDB as `Decimal128` rather than a plain number?

choices.text: A plain number cannot hold more than two decimal places
choices.why: It holds many; the problem is that 39.90 has no exact binary form.

choices.text: It takes less space on disk
choices.why: Space is not the reason given.

choices.text: Indexes do not work on plain numbers, so a price range would be a full scan
choices.why: They do; precision is the point.

choices.text: It stores decimal digits, so 268.80 is kept exactly as typed
choices.why: Right.

prompt: A relational shop answers an analyst's new question months after launch with no schema change. What makes that possible, and what do the stores of this course give up?

choices.text: Normalisation keeps every fact in two tables; these stores keep one
choices.why: Normalisation is each fact in exactly one place.

choices.text: The join and the planner, at read time; the stores here give them up across machines
choices.why: Right: across machines a join is a network trip per row, so the questions move from read time to design time.

choices.text: Foreign keys
choices.why: Foreign keys protect the data; they do not answer a question.

choices.text: A stored copy of every past query result, which the stores of this course keep only in memory
choices.why: Nothing was stored in advance; the answer was computed when the question arrived.

prompt: A Cassandra table has `PRIMARY KEY ((customer), ordered_at)`. Ana places two orders that get the same timestamp. What does a `SELECT` of her partition show afterwards?

choices.text: Both orders, side by side, with the later one first
choices.why: Two rows need two keys, and these two had one.

choices.text: Only the second order: the first was overwritten without an error
choices.why: Right: an INSERT for a key that exists overwrites it, and there is no duplicate check.

choices.text: Only the first order, because the second insert was refused as a duplicate key
choices.why: Checking would mean a read before every write, which the write path avoids.

choices.text: Neither, until a repair settles which one wins
choices.why: There is one node and no disagreement; the second write simply replaced the first.

prompt: A product page shows the product with its reviews ten at a time on a page of their own, and a popular product collects thousands. Where do the reviews go in MongoDB?

choices.text: Embedded in the product, so one read returns everything the page needs
choices.why: They are not read with the product, and an unbounded list heads for the 16 MB wall.

choices.text: In documents of their own that hold the product's key
choices.why: Right: unbounded and read separately, so referenced.

choices.text: Embedded, split across several fields of the product
choices.why: Several fields are still one document, under one size limit.

choices.text: In Redis, because MongoDB refuses lists longer than a thousand items
choices.why: The limit is on the document's size in bytes, not on the length of a list.

prompt: On a Redis holding a million keys, `KEYS cart:*` and a `SCAN` loop both found the one basket. What did `INFO commandstats` show? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: KEYS was one call of about 139 ms, and every other client waited through it
choices.why: Right: Redis runs commands one at a time.

choices.text: SCAN spent more time in total than KEYS
choices.why: Right: about 273 ms against 139, in pauses of a few hundred microseconds.

choices.text: SCAN was faster in total, which is why it is preferred
choices.why: It was slower in total; what it shortens is the longest single pause.

choices.text: KEYS ran on a background thread and blocked nobody
choices.why: Nothing ran beside it: for 139 ms the server did nothing else.

prompt: Cassandra refused `ORDER BY` on `orders_by_customer`: it is only supported when the ___ key is restricted by an EQ or an IN, because order exists inside one and nowhere else.
The mouse goes up from 189.00 to 199.00 in `products`. Order 1001's line still says `unit_price: 189.00`. What is the right reading?

choices.text: A drifted copy, which the scheduled check should repair from `products`
choices.why: Repairing it would be the worst bug in the shop: a bill Ana never agreed to.

choices.text: Correct: a snapshot of what Ana paid
choices.why: Right: it must not follow the price list; an invoice, a refund and a dispute all need the price of the day.

choices.text: A sign that the `updateMany` after the price change was forgotten
choices.why: No `updateMany` belongs there; this copy is updated by nothing, ever.

choices.text: MongoDB delays propagating a change to embedded copies
choices.why: MongoDB knows nothing about copies; nothing propagates by itself.

prompt: By lesson 4's trade, which fact is a poor candidate to copy into the documents the order page reads?

choices.text: A product's name
choices.why: It changes a few times a year and is read all day: the copy pays.

choices.text: The customer's name
choices.why: Rarely changed, shown on every view: the extended reference of the lesson.

choices.text: A stock count that moves with every sale
choices.why: Right: changed all the time and read rarely, so every sale would pay to update the copies.

choices.text: The price the customer paid
choices.why: That one is copied as a snapshot and never changes.

prompt: Match each copy in the shop to what updates it.

pairs.right: nothing, ever: the price as paid
nothing: the name as sold
`updateMany` on `customer.id` after the rename
`updateMany` with `arrayFilters` on the item's SKU

right_distractors: a trigger MongoDB runs whenever the source changes

prompt: An order is written to `orders_by_id` and `orders_by_customer` in one logged batch. Which are true? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: If the coordinator dies halfway, another node replays the rest from the batch log
choices.why: Right: all or nothing, eventually.

choices.text: A reader can see the order in one table before it appears in the other
choices.why: Right: there is no isolation; the two writes are not one moment.

choices.text: It is faster than the two inserts on their own
choices.why: Writing the batch log first is an extra round of writes.

choices.text: A statement that fails after the batch was accepted rolls the others back
choices.why: Once accepted, a batch is applied, not undone.

prompt: Bruno's order must be inserted exactly once, in both tables. A batch with `IF NOT EXISTS` on each insert is refused: `Batch with conditions cannot span multiple tables`. What does lesson 4 do instead?

choices.text: A conditional insert into `orders_by_id`, then the copy
choices.why: Right: one table owns the identity, and the copy is written only if that insert succeeded.

choices.text: The same batch without the conditions, sent at `ALL`
choices.why: A level decides how many replicas answer, not whether the order already exists.

choices.text: Two conditional batches, one per table
choices.why: Then the second can fail after the first succeeded, with nobody deciding which table is the truth.

choices.text: An unlogged batch, which accepts conditions across tables
choices.why: A condition is a lightweight transaction, which runs against one partition of one table.

prompt: After the repair, the drift check `db.carts.aggregate([unwind, join, differ, { $count: "drifted" }])` printed nothing at all. How should a script that alerts on it read that?

choices.text: As a failure to run, and alert
choices.why: It ran; that is how a clean run looks.

choices.text: As zero drifted copies
choices.why: Right: `$count` makes a document only when something reaches it, so no document means 0.

choices.text: As a sign that `$lookup` found no products
choices.why: Then every item would differ and the count would be high.

choices.text: As unknown, until the check is run on a secondary
choices.why: Running it on a secondary keeps it cheap; it does not change the answer.

prompt: A Redis replica was cut off from its primary, and the stock changed on the primary. Long after `master_link_status` turned `down`, `GET` on the replica still answered the old stock. Why?

choices.text: `replica-serve-stale-data` is `yes` by default
choices.why: Right: a replica that knows it is cut off still serves what it has; set to `no`, it would refuse instead. The CAP choice in one line.

choices.text: The replica had not yet noticed, because `repl-timeout` had not passed
choices.why: That explains the first read, while the link still said `up`; this one came after.

choices.text: The replica cached the key and served it from the cache
choices.why: It served its own copy of the data; there is no separate cache.

choices.text: The write on the primary had been rolled back
choices.why: Once reconnected, the replica answered 0, the primary's value.

prompt: Match each anomaly to what the user sees.

pairs.right: Ana saves a new address and the reload shows the old one
an order shown as shipped, then as paid again
two checkouts sell the last monitor and the stock says one was sold

right_distractors: a write refused with an error until the replica catches up

prompt: A payment insert times out, and the client retries it with the same `_id`, `pay-1001-a7f3`, which it chose before the first attempt. The retry answers `E11000 duplicate key error`. What should the application conclude?

choices.text: The payment failed and must be retried with a new id
choices.why: A new id would charge the customer twice.

choices.text: The payment is already done
choices.why: Right: the first attempt landed, and here the duplicate-key error is the success case.

choices.text: The collection is corrupt and needs a repair
choices.why: The unique `_id` index did exactly its job.

choices.text: A different order already used that id
choices.why: The count for order 1001 was 1: its own first attempt.

prompt: Two checkouts both read the monitor at `version: 1` and both send `updateOne({ _id: "MN-330", version: 1 }, { $inc: { stock: -1, version: 1 } })`. What does the second one get, and what must the application do?

choices.text: A write-conflict error, which the driver retries by itself
choices.why: No error is raised at all.

choices.text: `matchedCount: 1`, with stock taken to -1
choices.why: Version 1 no longer existed, so nothing matched.

choices.text: `matchedCount: 0`; read the product again and decide afresh
choices.why: Right: that zero is the whole mechanism of optimistic concurrency.

choices.text: A lock until the first checkout commits
choices.why: Nobody locks anything; the conflict is detected at write time.

prompt: In Cassandra, an update stamped with a timestamp from late 2027 sets a price of 159.00. An ordinary update made now sets 199.00. What does a `SELECT` return?

choices.text: 199.00, because it arrived last
choices.why: Arrival order decides nothing; the higher timestamp wins.

choices.text: 159.00, until real time passes 2027
choices.why: Right: every ordinary correction loses the same way, and both updates were told they succeeded.

choices.text: An error, because a timestamp in the future is refused
choices.why: It was accepted without a word.

choices.text: Both values, for the application to choose
choices.why: Last write wins keeps one value per cell.

prompt: `db.orders.updateOne({ _id: 22 }, { $set: { status: "paid" } })` names an order that does not exist. What does MongoDB answer?

choices.text: An error saying the document was not found
choices.why: No error is raised; an application that waits for one reports the order as paid.

choices.text: `acknowledged: true` with `matchedCount: 0`
choices.why: Right: the server changed every order with that id, which was none. The count is the result.

choices.text: It inserts order 22 with the status paid
choices.why: That needs `upsert: true`, and this call did not ask for it.

choices.text: `acknowledged: false`, because nothing was written to disk
choices.why: The write was acknowledged; it simply matched nothing.

prompt: An import stored one product's price as the string `"79.90"`. The page "products under 100" runs `find({ price: { $lt: NumberDecimal("100") } })`. What happens to that product?

choices.text: The query fails with a type mismatch, naming the document
choices.why: That is what `$multiply` did in the tax report. This query did not fail.

choices.text: It is listed, because MongoDB converts the string to a number to compare
choices.why: No conversion happens; types are compared first.

choices.text: It is left out, silently
choices.why: Right: values are compared by type first, and a range of numbers holds no string. A short list, and nothing on the page looks wrong.

choices.text: It is listed last, after every number
choices.why: A string sorts after every number in a sort; a numeric range filters it out altogether.

prompt: A product does not exist. A client runs `updateOne({ _id: "LS-050" }, { $set: { name: "Laptop stand" }, $inc: { stock: 5 } }, { upsert: true })`, times out, and retries the same call once. What is the stock now?
A validator is being added to a collection that programs are already writing to, and some stored documents break it. Put the rollout in order.
items: Attach the rule with `validationAction: "warn"`
Read the server's log for "would fail validation" for a few days
Repair the documents until the `$nor` census returns 0
Switch to `validationLevel: "strict"` and `validationAction: "error"`
trap: Refusing before the census is empty stops a working application from updating its own documents.

prompt: A shop puts each customer's ObjectId in the address of their profile page. What does a stranger who reads the address learn?

choices.text: Nothing; an ObjectId is twelve random bytes
choices.why: The first four bytes are a clock, and the counter makes neighbours easy to guess.

choices.text: Which shard of the cluster holds the customer
choices.why: The id carries a time and a counter, not a location in a cluster.

choices.text: When the account was created, to the second
choices.why: Right: `getTimestamp()` reads the first four bytes back. An id is not a secret.

choices.text: The customer's e-mail, encoded in hexadecimal
choices.why: The id is made by the client from a clock and a counter, not from the document's fields.

prompt: The warehouse asks for pending orders of 3,000 or more, the newest twenty: `find({ status: "pending", total: { $gte: 3000 } }).sort({ ordered_at: -1 })`. Put the fields of the index that reads fewest entries in order, first field first.
items: `status`
`ordered_at`
`total`
trap: Equality, then sort, then range: with the range before the sort, a SORT stage reads all 1,139 matches to keep twenty.

prompt: For March's pending orders, `{ ordered_at: -1, status: 1 }` read 8,574 index entries and `{ status: 1, ordered_at: -1 }` read 339, for the same 339 orders. Why?

choices.text: Descending fields have to be read twice, once in each direction
choices.why: A one-field direction does not matter; the server walks an index either way.

choices.text: Date first, March holds every status mixed together
choices.why: Right: the scan walks all of March and keeps the pending ones; status first, they sit together.

choices.text: The first index was not yet finished building when the query ran
choices.why: Both were complete; the difference is the order of their fields.

choices.text: A hint costs extra reads
choices.why: Both queries carried a hint, and only one read too much.

prompt: Ana's history query is covered: `PROJECTION_COVERED <- IXSCAN`, `docs: 0`. Somebody removes `_id: 0` from its projection. What happens?

choices.text: The query is refused, because a covered projection cannot name `_id`
choices.why: Nothing is refused; that is what makes it fragile.

choices.text: The planner drops the index and scans all 100,000 orders
choices.why: The index is still used to find the 82 entries.

choices.text: The same 82 orders come back, now with a FETCH that opens each document for its `_id`
choices.why: Right: `_id` is not in that index, and nothing fails to tell you.

choices.text: The orders come back without `_id`, since the index holds none
choices.why: `_id` comes back unless excluded, so the server reads the documents to find it.

prompt: Application code queries paid orders with `.hint("pending_by_date")`, a partial index whose filter is `status: "pending"`. What does it get?

choices.text: An error saying the index cannot serve the query
choices.why: There is no error, which is the danger.

choices.text: Twenty paid orders, because the planner ignores a hint that does not fit
choices.why: A hint is obeyed; the planner leaves a partial index alone only when nobody forces it.

choices.text: No orders, and no error
choices.why: Right: it read all 4,044 pending entries, kept none, and did not complain.

choices.text: The twenty newest pending orders
choices.why: The filter still applies to what is read; none of the pending entries is paid.

prompt: An order has three lines: `CB-012`, `MS-204` and `CB-012` again. How many entries does it put in a multikey index on `items.sku`?
A session collection has a TTL index with `expireAfterSeconds: 300` on `last_seen`. When does a session last seen six minutes ago leave the collection?

choices.text: It left at exactly the 300th second
choices.why: Nothing deletes on the second; a task sweeps for expired documents.

choices.text: At the next pass of a background task that runs once a minute
choices.why: Right: up to a minute late, longer on a busy server, so code that must not see it checks the date itself.

choices.text: The next time a query reads it
choices.why: Reading does not delete; the background task does.

choices.text: Only after the server restarts
choices.why: The lab's expired session was gone seventy seconds later, with no restart.

prompt: Every order was placed in 2026 by the generator's UTC clock, yet revenue per month, grouped with `timezone: "America/Sao_Paulo"`, starts with `2025-12` and 33 orders. Why?

choices.text: The generator has an off-by-one bug in its dates
choices.why: The dates are right; the question asked about another zone.

choices.text: In São Paulo those orders fell on 31 December
choices.why: Right: before 03:00 UTC on 1 January it was still December there. The zone belongs in the query.

choices.text: BSON stores each date with the zone of the client that wrote it
choices.why: A BSON date is a moment with no zone attached.

choices.text: `$sort` placed them first because `$group` ran in the wrong order
choices.why: The sort only ordered the months; the month itself came from the zone.

prompt: The loop in mongosh totalled 206042969.6000362; the pipeline returned `Decimal128('206042969.60')`. What made the loop wrong?

choices.text: It read some orders twice while the collection was being written
choices.why: Both counted 98,958 orders.

choices.text: `parseFloat` made each decimal a double
choices.why: Right: every addition carried a binary rounding error; the pipeline added where the type is exact.

choices.text: The pipeline rounds its sums to two places
choices.why: It rounds nothing: a sum of decimals is exact to the cent.

choices.text: The bytes crossing the connection lost precision on the way
choices.why: The documents arrived intact; the conversion in the program did the damage.

prompt: Put the stages of the best-sellers pipeline in the order lesson 8 runs them.

prompt: With an index on `{ status: 1, ordered_at: -1 }`, which pipeline was planned as a `COLLSCAN`?

choices.text: `$match` on `status: "pending"`, then `$group` by customer
choices.why: A match first became an index scan.

choices.text: `$group` by `status`, then `$match` on `_id: "pending"`
choices.why: The server moved that match in front of the group, and even covered it.

choices.text: `$group` by customer pushing statuses, then `$match` on `statuses: "pending"`
choices.why: Right: that match is on something the group computed, so it cannot move.

choices.text: None: a pipeline never reaches an index

prompt: A `$sort` with no index to serve it needs about 300 MB on MongoDB 8.0, with the default options. What happens?

choices.why: That needs `allowDiskUse: false`; the default has been on since 6.0.

choices.text: It uses the 300 MB, since the limit applies to the whole pipeline
choices.why: The 100 MB is per stage.

choices.text: It returns the first 100 MB of sorted results
choices.why: Nothing is truncated silently; it spills or fails.

choices.text: It spills to temporary files on disk
choices.why: Right: the explain shows `usedDisk: true`, slower than memory, and a sign an index or an earlier `$match` was missing.

prompt: Inside a pipeline stage, a field of the passing document is written with a ___ sign in front of its name, as in `"$total"`; written as `"total"`, a `$sum` adds nothing, silently.
With both secondaries frozen, an insert with `w: "majority", wtimeout: 3000` failed with `WriteConcernFailed` after three seconds. What state is the document in?

choices.text: It was undone when the timeout fired
choices.why: A write-concern error undoes nothing; the count went up to three.

choices.text: On the primary, with no promise it survives
choices.why: Right: the server could not confirm the guarantee in time. A blind retry writes twice.

choices.text: It was never written, because the primary checks the secondaries first
choices.why: The primary writes first and waits afterwards; the waiting is what timed out.

choices.text: It waits in the driver and is sent again when the secondaries unlock
choices.why: The driver received an error; nothing queues the write for later.

prompt: A replica-set primary is killed. By default, how many seconds without a heartbeat from it does a secondary wait before calling an election?
A price changed on the primary with `w: 1` while both secondaries were frozen. On the primary, a read with `readConcern("majority")` returned the old price. What does that show?

choices.text: Read concern `majority` sends the read to a secondary
choices.why: Where a read goes is read preference; this one ran on the primary.

choices.text: The new price was lost and will not come back
choices.why: Once unlocked, the same read returned 329.90.

choices.text: It buys durability, not freshness
choices.why: Right: it returns only what a majority has, older than `local`, and never a value about to disappear.

choices.text: The primary's cache had not been refreshed
choices.why: `local` on the same member saw the new price at the same instant.

prompt: A primary cut off from the other two accepted Ana's order with `w: 1`, then stepped down. The others elected a new primary and took Bruno's order. After the cable returns, where is Ana's order?

choices.text: Merged into the collection beside Bruno's
choices.why: Nothing merges two histories; the minority's is undone.

choices.text: In a rollback file on the old primary, applied by nobody unless a person does it
choices.why: Right: `/data/db/rollback`, readable with `bsondump`.

choices.text: In the collection, because the old primary takes its job back
choices.why: It rejoins as a secondary; nothing in the configuration prefers it.

choices.text: Only on the old primary, which keeps it as a local extra
choices.why: A member cannot keep a history the set does not have; it rolls back to the common point.

prompt: Match each read preference to where a read goes.

pairs.right: the primary; with none, the read fails
the primary, and a secondary only while there is none
a secondary, and the primary only while no secondary answers
whichever member answers fastest, primary or not

right_distractors: every member at once, and the newest answer wins

prompt: The shop's orders no longer fit on one machine's disk. Why does adding secondaries to the replica set not help?

choices.text: Secondaries cannot take reads
choices.why: They can, with a read preference; the problem is storage and writes.

choices.text: A replica set may hold at most three members
choices.why: Three is the smallest that works, not a ceiling.

choices.text: Each new member is another full copy
choices.why: Right: a replica set multiplies safety, not capacity.

choices.text: Secondaries compress their data, which is slower to read
choices.why: A secondary holds the same data as the primary, the same way.

prompt: `orders` is sharded on `{ orderId: 1 }`, split at 5001, with the upper range on `shard2`. Orders 10001 to 20000 arrive. Where do they go?

choices.text: Half to each shard, as the first ten thousand did
choices.why: The first ten thousand straddled 5001; these are all above it.

choices.text: All to `shard2`, the top range
choices.why: Right: a growing number always lands in the top range, and moving that range only moves the hot spot.

choices.text: To whichever shard holds fewer documents at the moment

prompt: A dump runs while payments are still arriving. What does `mongodump --oplog` add to it?

prompt: Two workers each read a stock counter with GET, add one in the application and SET it back, 500 times each. Why did fewer than 1,000 increments survive?

choices.why: Every SET was applied; some carried a stale value.

choices.text: Both read the same value and wrote the same sum
choices.why: Right: one increment overwrote the other, a lost update. INCR does the read and the write in one command.

choices.text: The counter expired halfway through
choices.why: No expiry was set.

choices.text: Redis runs commands on several threads at once
choices.why: It runs them one at a time; the race is in the application.

prompt: A key has a TTL. The application overwrites its value with a plain `SET`. What does `TTL` answer afterwards?

choices.text: The remaining seconds, unchanged
choices.why: A plain SET discards the expiry.

choices.text: -2, because the key was deleted
choices.why: -2 means the key does not exist; it does.

choices.text: -1: the key now lives for ever

prompt: A worker in a consumer group read an order event with XREADGROUP and crashed before XACK. Where is the event now?

choices.text: Gone, because reading removed it from the stream

choices.text: In the group's pending list, under that worker
choices.why: Right: it stays there until acknowledged; XPENDING shows it and XAUTOCLAIM hands it to another worker.

choices.text: Delivered again to every worker of the group
choices.why: A group gives each entry to one worker.

choices.text: Back at the end of the stream with a new id
choices.why: Entries keep their id; nothing re-appends them.

prompt: Which structure keeps a best-seller ranking up to date on every sale?

choices.text: A set with SADD
choices.why: A set has no order and no number.

choices.text: A hash with one field per product
choices.why: It can count, but cannot return the top three in order.

choices.text: A sorted set with ZINCRBY
choices.why: Right: the members stay ordered by score.

prompt: Put a consumer group's handling of one order event in order.
items: XADD appends the event to the stream
XREADGROUP hands it to one worker
The event waits in the pending list
The worker finishes and sends XACK

prompt: A Redis with snapshots only is tested by writing a key after the last `BGSAVE` and restarting it with `docker stop`. The key is still there. Why does the test prove little?

choices.text: Redis wrote a final snapshot on SIGTERM

prompt: Match each persistence setting to what the machine losing power costs, as Redis's documentation states it.

pairs.right: every write since the last snapshot
nothing that was acknowledged
about the last second of writes
whatever the operating system had not yet flushed

prompt: A Redis has run with snapshots only for a year. The team wants the append-only file on without losing a key. What is the safe way?

choices.text: Restart the container with `--appendonly yes`; Redis loads `dump.rdb` and then starts the log
choices.why: With the log on, Redis loads only the log: it made an empty one and started with nothing.

choices.text: `CONFIG SET appendonly yes` on the running server, wait for the base file, then restart with the flag
choices.why: Right: the base is written from memory first, and the flag keeps the log on after restarts.

choices.text: Delete `dump.rdb` first, so the two files cannot disagree
choices.why: That deletes the only copy of the data on disk.

choices.text: Copy `dump.rdb` into `appendonlydir` and restart

prompt: Ten thousand `INCR` commands on one counter grew the incremental AOF file to 330,188 bytes. What does `BGREWRITEAOF` leave behind?

choices.why: Right: the sequence goes to 2, and the value already includes the increments, so they go.

choices.why: A rewrite works from what is in memory, not from the age of commands.

choices.text: A single `dump.rdb`, and the log switched off

prompt: A snapshot failed on a full disk, and now every `SET` answers `MISCONF`. What does lesson 13 say the cure is?

choices.why: That accepts writes Redis cannot save, promising a durability it does not have.

choices.text: Restart Redis to clear the error
choices.why: The next snapshot fails the same way on the same disk.

choices.text: Switch `appendfsync` to `always`
choices.why: A log needs the same disk the snapshot could not write to.

choices.text: Fix the disk, so that a snapshot succeeds
choices.why: Right: the cure is the disk, not the setting. Writes resume once a snapshot succeeds.

prompt: With `appendfsync everysec`, a `docker kill` lost no write even within the last second, because the bytes `write()` had handed over sat in the operating system's page ___, which the kernel still flushed.
A Redis runs `volatile-lru` at its `maxmemory`, and one service writes its cache pages with a plain `SET` and no `EX`. What does that service see when the instance is full?

choices.text: Its oldest pages are evicted, as the policy's name says
choices.why: Only keys with an expiry may go under `volatile-`, and these have none.

choices.text: `OOM` errors on its writes, and `evicted_keys` stays at 0
choices.why: Right: no candidate, so Redis refuses exactly as `noeviction` would.

choices.text: The products, which also have no expiry, are evicted to make room
choices.why: A key without an expiry is never a candidate under `volatile-`.

choices.text: Redis gives each page a default expiry of one hour

choices.text: The products had an expiry, and `allkeys-random` prefers keys with one

choices.text: Random treats a hot product like a page nobody reads

choices.text: LRU keeps a perfect ordering of every key

prompt: A sensor writes a reading every second, and the screen shows one sensor's readings, newest first. Which primary key keeps every partition bounded?

prompt: In Ana's partition, `ORDER BY ordered_at ASC` works and `ORDER BY total DESC` is refused. Why the difference?

prompt: A keyspace keeps three copies. Which pairs of write level and read level make a read see the last acknowledged write? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: write `ONE`, read `ALL`
choices.why: Right: 1 + 3 > 3; writes are cheap and any node down stops every read.

prompt: A Cassandra table is used as a queue: 1500 emails inserted into one partition, 1499 deleted once sent. Each poll returns one row and steps over 1499 tombstones. Which change stops that?

choices.text: A worker that remembers how far it got instead of deleting what it handled

choices.text: An SAI index on `id`

`gc_grace_seconds` passes with no repair

prompt: A deleted wish-list item came back on all three nodes after a repair. What does lesson 18 say actually went wrong?

choices.why: It did its job with what it was given: a row on one replica and nothing on the others.

choices.text: The tombstone expired before it reached every replica
choices.why: Right: no record was left to say the row had been deleted.

choices.text: The delete should have been sent at `ONE`
choices.why: A lower level reaches fewer replicas, not more.

choices.text: Compaction should never drop a tombstone
choices.why: Then a table that deletes would grow without end; purging after the grace period is correct.

prompt: A Cassandra node has been down for two weeks, longer than its tables' `gc_grace_seconds`. What is the standard advice?

choices.text: Start it and run a full repair at once
choices.why: That repair is how its forgotten rows reach everybody else.

choices.text: Raise `gc_grace_seconds` on every table, then start it
choices.why: The tombstones already purged do not come back.

choices.text: Start it and serve reads at `ONE` until it catches up
choices.why: A read at `ONE` that reaches it returns rows everyone else deleted.

choices.text: Wipe it and let it rejoin as a new node
choices.why: Right: its data may hold rows whose deletes the others have forgotten.

prompt: Match each compaction strategy to the table it suits.

pairs.right: write-heavy tables, merged in tiers of similar size
read-heavy tables whose rows are updated often
time series written once and expired by TTL
new clusters on 5.0, as `cassandra_latest.yaml` recommends

right_distractors: tables that are never deleted from, with tombstones turned off

prompt: With `c3` down, two writes at `QUORUM` left a file named after `c3`'s host ID in `c1`'s hints directory, while `nodetool listpendinghints` answered that there were none. What does lesson 19 conclude?

choices.text: The writes were lost, since no hint is pending
choices.why: The file was replayed to `c3` when it returned, and then deleted.

choices.text: Trust the directory, whose file names say whom they are for
choices.why: Right: a tool that says nothing is easy to believe during an incident.

choices.text: The file is a leftover from an earlier run and can be deleted
choices.why: It held these two updates; deleting it would have lost them for `c3`.

choices.text: Hinted handoff was switched off on `c1`
choices.why: `statushandoff` said it was running, and the file proves it.

prompt: Match each mechanism to the gap it leaves.

pairs.right: a node down longer than `max_hint_window`
rows nobody reads, and reads at `ONE`
none, provided it runs within `gc_grace_seconds`

prompt: `c3` holds 5 units for the keyboard and the other two hold 4. Which read repairs `c3`?

choices.text: Any read of the row at `ONE`, wherever it lands
choices.why: A read at `ONE` asks one replica and compares nothing.

choices.text: A read that asks `c3` and another replica, finds a digest mismatch and writes the newest value back
choices.why: Right: the trace showed `read-repair-mutation` sent to `c3`.

choices.text: A read of any other row in the same table
choices.why: Read repair fixes the rows read, not their neighbours.

choices.text: A read at `QUORUM` that happens to ask only `c1` and `c2`
choices.why: They agree, so there is nothing to repair, and `c3` stays behind.

prompt: A schedule runs `nodetool repair -pr` on every node in turn. Why `-pr`?

choices.text: It repairs only the ranges the node owns as first replica, so one pass over all nodes covers each range once
choices.why: Right: without it, with three copies, each range is repaired three times.

choices.text: It runs the repair in parallel on all nodes at once
choices.why: The schedule runs one node at a time on purpose; repair reads and streams a lot.

choices.text: It makes the repair incremental
choices.why: Incremental is the default without `-full`; `-pr` is about which ranges.

choices.text: It skips the Merkle trees
choices.why: Every repair compares trees; that is how it avoids sending everything.

prompt: A team runs incremental repairs often. Why does lesson 19 still advise a full repair now and then?

choices.text: Incremental repair does not build Merkle trees
choices.why: It compares the same way, over the SSTables not yet stamped.

choices.text: An incremental repair ignores tables with tombstones
choices.why: Nothing in it excludes tombstones.

choices.text: It trusts the repaired stamp
choices.why: Right: data damaged after being marked is never looked at again. Incremental often, full now and then.

choices.text: Incremental repair works on one table per run
choices.why: It takes a keyspace or a table, like a full one.

prompt: Lesson 19 says to alert when a node's last successful repair is older than the schedule's period, not only when a repair fails. Why?

choices.text: A failed repair writes no log line
choices.why: A failure is logged; the trouble is a repair that never starts.

choices.text: A repair that never starts never fails
choices.why: Right: a broken job, a departed person, and nothing errors until a deleted row returns.

choices.text: Cassandra 5.0 repairs itself, so failures are rare
choices.why: Its auto-repair service was disabled; repair is somebody's job.

choices.text: Read repair already covers the failures
choices.why: It covers only rows that are read, at levels that ask more than one replica.

prompt: A Redis replica was paused while the primary took writes. `INFO replication` showed `state=online`, `lag=2`, and offsets 51,825,418 bytes apart. Which of these should the alert watch?

choices.text: `lag`, since two seconds is already more than one
choices.why: `lag` is the seconds since the replica last acknowledged anything; a slow replica keeps it small.

choices.text: `state`, which turns to offline when the replica is behind
choices.why: It said `online` throughout.

choices.text: The primary's write latency, which climbs when a replica stops reading
choices.why: Writes ran at 127,388 a second with a p99 of 0.655 ms; the primary does not wait.

choices.text: The byte gap between the two offsets
choices.why: Right: about 49 MiB of writes that a primary dying then would lose.

prompt: A Redis cache reports `keyspace_hits:122951` and `keyspace_misses:93717`. What is its hit ratio, as a percentage to one decimal place?
`mongostat` printed `SLV` in its `repl` column on every line, and `rs.status()` said the same member was `PRIMARY`. What does lesson 20 conclude?

choices.text: The member was flapping between the two roles every second
choices.why: `rs.status()` before and after showed one stable primary.

choices.text: The tool reports the role wrongly against an 8.0 server, so the role is taken from `rs.status()`
choices.why: Right: a monitoring tool is software with bugs of its own.

choices.text: `mongostat` was connected to a secondary by mistake
choices.why: It ran inside the primary's own container, against that server.

choices.text: `rs.status()` is cached and lags the real role
choices.why: It is the replica set's own answer, built from heartbeats every two seconds.

prompt: Which of these should page somebody at three in the morning, by lesson 20's two questions? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A Cassandra node `DN` for longer than `max_hint_window`
choices.why: Right: past it, only repair restores the writes it missed.

choices.text: A Redis under `noeviction` with `used_memory` at `maxmemory`
choices.why: Right: writes are failing with `OOM`.

choices.text: A Redis cache under `allkeys-lru` at 97% of its memory
choices.why: That is what a cache with a limit looks like.

choices.text: A MongoDB secondary 18 seconds behind on a quiet afternoon
choices.why: Nobody is harmed and it catches up by itself; it pages when it nears the oplog window.

choices.text: A replica set with no member `PRIMARY`
choices.why: Right: writes are being refused.

prompt: `nodetool tpstats` on one replica shows a rising count of dropped `MUTATION_REQ`. What has happened to those writes?

choices.text: The clients were told they failed, and retried
choices.why: The client may have been told yes, at a level other replicas satisfied.

choices.text: This replica threw them away after their timeout
choices.why: Right: its copy is missing until repair, which is why it pages at a sustained rate.

choices.text: They were queued as hints on this replica
choices.why: Hints are kept by a coordinator for a node that is down; this node was up and dropped them.

choices.text: They are still pending and will run when the stage frees up
choices.why: Pending is a separate column; dropped means discarded.

prompt: A team moves its databases to managed services. Which of these are still the team's to decide or do? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The shard key
choices.why: Right: fixed at creation, and the provider accepts a bad one.

choices.text: Whether Redis evicts, and by which policy
choices.why: Right: the same full memory is fine for a cache and data loss for a database.

choices.text: Restore drills
choices.why: Right: the provider's backup is a hope until somebody restores it.

choices.text: Replacing a disk that died
choices.why: Below the line: the node is rebuilt from its peers without a ticket from you.

choices.text: Applying operating-system security fixes
choices.why: The provider applies them in a window you choose.

prompt: Amazon DocumentDB is described as compatible with MongoDB. What does that mean, by lesson 21?

choices.text: MongoDB itself, run on Amazon's machines
choices.why: That is what Atlas offers; DocumentDB does not run MongoDB.

choices.text: Amazon's own engine behind a MongoDB-speaking layer
choices.why: Right: it publishes what it does not support; read that list before migrating, not in production after.

choices.text: A licensed fork of MongoDB 8.0
choices.why: It is not a fork; it is another engine with a translation in front.

choices.text: Any MongoDB driver works, so behaviour under load is identical
choices.why: The engine underneath differs, and so does its behaviour under load.

prompt: A dump reads at 40 MB/s. Counting 1 TB as 1,000,000 MB, how many hours does dumping 2 TB take, before the restore and its index builds?
Match each product to its licence as lesson 21 states it.

pairs.right: the Server Side Public License
RSALv2 or SSPLv1, a dual licence
BSD, as the fork of Redis 7.2.4
Apache License 2.0

prompt: The shop stores its orders in MongoDB, which is under the SSPL. What does the licence require of the shop?

choices.text: Publishing the source of the whole shop
choices.why: That obligation falls on offering the database itself as a service to others.

choices.text: A commercial licence once the shop has paying customers
choices.why: Running it for your own application is allowed, paying customers or not.

choices.text: Nothing beyond the ordinary: running it for its own application is allowed
choices.why: Right: the SSPL restricts offering MongoDB as a service, which the shop is not doing.

choices.text: Using MongoDB Atlas rather than running its own
choices.why: The course ran `mongo:8.0` itself, which the licence allows.

prompt: A managed MongoDB promotes a new primary in seconds. What part of that failover is still the application's?

choices.text: Choosing which secondary is promoted
choices.why: The election still happens between the members the provider built.

choices.text: Rebuilding the old primary's node
choices.why: Below the line: the provider replaces machines.

choices.text: Nothing; the provider replays the dropped writes
choices.why: No service can write that code for you.

choices.text: Reconnecting, and retrying the writes that got errors while it happened
choices.why: Right: as in lessons 9 and 15.

prompt: The shop commits an order in Postgres and then `SET`s the new stock in Redis. A deploy kills the process between the two. What does lesson 22 put in place of this dual write?

choices.text: Write to Redis first and commit in Postgres afterwards, the other way round
choices.why: The other order only changes which side is wrong.

choices.text: Retry the `SET` until Redis answers
choices.why: The process that would retry is the one that died.

choices.text: An outbox row in the same commit, applied by a relay
choices.why: Right: either both rows exist or neither does.

choices.text: Run Redis with `appendfsync always`
choices.why: Redis never heard the write; durability there does not help.

prompt: Outbox entries say "set the stock of MN-330 to 0" rather than "decrement the stock of MN-330". Why?

choices.text: Redis has no command that decrements
choices.why: It has `DECR`; lesson 12 used it on stock.

choices.text: A set applied twice is harmless; a decrement is not
choices.why: Right: the relay delivers at least once, and one that dies after `SET` and before marking the entry applies it again.

choices.text: A set is smaller to store in the outbox
choices.why: Size is not the reason; repetition is.

choices.text: Postgres cannot store a negative number in the outbox
choices.why: It can; the entry is about what happens if it is applied twice.

prompt: Postgres held a `page_views` table and an `UNLOGGED` table `cache`. After `docker kill` and a restart, `page_views` had its row and `cache` was empty. Why?

choices.text: The cache entry had expired during the restart
choices.why: It had five minutes, and nothing in Postgres deletes expired rows by itself.

choices.text: An unlogged table skips the write-ahead log
choices.why: Right: recovery has nothing to replay for it and empties it; cheaper writes, and a cache allowed to come back empty.

choices.text: Recovery failed for that table and needs a manual repair
choices.why: This is documented behaviour, not a failure.

choices.text: `docker kill` deletes tables created with `ON CONFLICT`
choices.why: `page_views` was written with `ON CONFLICT` too, and survived.

prompt: A worker holds job 1 with `SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` inside an open transaction. A second worker runs the same query. What does it get?

choices.text: Job 1 too, since a read does not lock
choices.why: `FOR UPDATE` locks the row it returns.

choices.text: Nothing until the first worker commits, then job 1
choices.why: That is plain `FOR UPDATE`; `SKIP LOCKED` does not queue.

choices.text: Job 2, at once
choices.why: Right: locked rows are passed over, so two workers never take the same job.

choices.text: An error saying the table is locked
choices.why: The table held only a `RowShareLock`; the lock is on the row.

prompt: Which of these does lesson 22 list as things Postgres does not do as well? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Taking writes on many machines at once
choices.why: Right: one primary takes every write.

choices.text: Accepting writes in two regions at the same moment
choices.why: Right: its answer is one region that writes and readers elsewhere.

choices.text: Sorted sets and streams at memory speed
choices.why: Right: a table with an index is a good counter and a slower leaderboard.

choices.text: Querying documents of varying shape through an index
choices.why: `jsonb` with a GIN index answered `@>` with a bitmap index scan.

choices.text: A queue where two workers never take the same job
choices.why: `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` does exactly that.

prompt: The order is an aggregate, which sounds like MongoDB's case. Why does the shop's decision record keep orders in Postgres?

choices.text: MongoDB cannot store an order with its items inside it
choices.why: Lesson 2 stored exactly that.

choices.text: The order changes in the same transaction as stock and payment, and the reports join it to everything
choices.why: Right: several entities changed together is the relational row of the table.

choices.text: The write volume is too high for MongoDB
choices.why: It is thousands a day; volume was the argument against Cassandra, the other way round.

choices.text: MongoDB's licence forbids shops from using it
choices.why: Running it for your own application is allowed.
